title: Names, Arrange-Act-Assert, one behaviour
summary: Tests that explain a red build: names that state the rule, the Arrange-Act-Assert shape, one behaviour per test, and the smells that make suites slow and brittle.

steps.title: A failing test is a message to a stranger
body: At 2 a.m. the build goes red and someone who has never seen your code reads this line in the CI log:
```text
Failed InvoiceTests.Test3 [12 ms]
Failed InvoiceTests.Late_fee_starts_on_day_15_not_day_14 [9 ms]
The second name tells them the rule and the broken case before they open a file. Name tests after **behaviour**, not methods. Two styles are common; pick one per codebase and stick to it:
- `Method_State_Expected`: `Cost_TotalIsFifty_ShipsFree`
- a sentence with underscores: `Fifty_euros_ships_free`, `Rejects_names_shorter_than_3_characters`
Inside, every test has the same three parts, separated by a blank line:
```csharp fragment
[Fact]
public void Late_fee_starts_on_day_15()
// Arrange: build exactly the world this case needs
var invoice = new Invoice(amount: 100m, due: new DateOnly(2026, 11, 1));
// Act: one call, the behaviour under test
decimal fee = invoice.LateFee(today: new DateOnly(2026, 11, 16));
// Assert: what must be true now
Assert.Equal(2.50m, fee);
One **Act** per test. If you need two acts, you have two behaviours, so write two tests.

steps.prompt: Put the test in Arrange-Act-Assert order.
steps.explain: Arrange builds a cart with one item, Act removes it, Assert checks the result. `Assert.Empty` reads better than `Assert.Equal(0, cart.Items.Count)` and prints the items when it fails.

steps.prompt: You open a CI log after a dependency upgrade. Which failing test name helps you most?
steps.explain: It names the rule and the condition, so you can guess the cause (a culture change in the upgrade) before reading any code. "Works correctly" says nothing a red test does not already say.

steps.title: One behaviour per test, and the smells to avoid
body: A test that checks five things stops at the first failure: you learn about one bug and the other four hide. Split it so each test has one reason to fail.

Several asserts are fine when they describe **one** outcome (`Assert.Equal("Ada", user.Name); Assert.Equal("ada@example.com", user.Email);`). xUnit v3's `Assert.Multiple(() => ..., () => ...)` runs them all and reports every failure together.
Smells that make suites slow, flaky or useless:
| Smell | Why it hurts | Instead |
| `if` or loops in a test | the test has its own bugs, and nobody tests the test | one test per case, or a `[Theory]` |
| `Thread.Sleep(500)` | slow, and still flaky on a busy CI agent | a fake clock, or await the real signal |
| tests sharing a static list | they pass alone and fail together, in some orders | fresh objects in each test |
| asserting on log text or private fields | breaks on every refactor | assert on results and public state |
| magic numbers (`Assert.Equal(42, ...)`) | the reader cannot see why 42 | name the inputs, or compute nothing in the assert |

steps.prompt: Match each smell to its fix.
pairs: a `foreach` over 12 inputs with one assert inside
a `static List<Order>` shared by every test
build fresh data in each test
split it into one test per behaviour
calling a private method through reflection
test it through the public method that uses it

steps.prompt: This test passes on Monday and fails on Saturday. What is wrong with it?
options: It reads the real clock, so its input changes every day: pass a fixed time (later: `TimeProvider` and `FakeTimeProvider`)
It should catch the exception and ignore it on weekends
steps.explain: A test must control every input. `DateTime.Now` is a hidden input, so the test checks a different case every day, and on Saturday the rule (ship Monday) is different. Module 3 replaces the clock with `FakeTimeProvider`.

steps.title: Test a sign-up rule, one behaviour per test
prompt: The sign-up form calls this, compiled beside your tests:
// 3 to 20 characters; letters, digits and '_'; must start with a letter.
Write `public class UsernameTests` with at least **five** `[Fact]` tests, each named after the one rule it checks, in Arrange-Act-Assert form. Use `Assert.True` and `Assert.False`.
Your tests run on this code and on five copies with one rule broken in each. Every rule has two edges: test the last value that is allowed and the first that is not.

mutants.name: two-character names are accepted
mutants.hint: Test a name of exactly 2 characters.

mutants.name: a name may start with a digit

hints: List the rules: minimum length, maximum length, first character, allowed characters. Each needs a test on the allowed side and on the refused side.
`new string('a', 20)` is the longest allowed name and `new string('a', 21)` the shortest refused one.
Do not forget the allowed underscore (`"ada_l"` is valid) and a refused character (`"ada-l"` is not).
steps.explain: Seven small tests, each with one reason to fail. When `Rejects_twenty_one_characters` goes red, nobody has to read the code to know which rule broke.
